entries.title: Democrats’ New Plan to Win in November: Just Be Normal
entries.summary: To win control of Congress, Democrats know they need voters who don’t love them.
entries.content:
Democrats are increasingly convinced that “double haters” — voters disappointed with both President Donald Trump and the Democratic Party — will make or break their chance at winning a House majority in November.

All it’ll take to win this voting group over, Democrats think, is one very normal trick.

In battleground districts across the country, Democratic candidates are attempting to prove that they are just like the average, everyday Americans they hope to represent. Their bet is that the promise of normalcy is enough to win over skeptical voters. It’s an effort that sits at the center of the party’s planned communication effort in the coming months, especially in the right-leaning seats its candidates need to win for a majority next year.

“What this really means is, are you putting your head down and working?” said Democratic Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet of Michigan. “Are you talking about things that really matter and using language that normal people use, not something from inside the beltway?”

McDonald Rivet, who won her Trump-supporting district with relative ease in 2024, is considered the template for the kind of candidate Democrats hope they recruited this year, a list that includes Rebecca Bennett in New Jersey, Zach Dembo in Kentucky and Chaz Molder in Tennessee.

In interviews, they described a formula for coming across as normal that included focusing on economic pressures instead of Trump’s actions and avoiding statements and positions more aligned with liberal activists than the larger body politic.

“The most important communication aspect of this is, ‘Hey, I’m a normal human being who’s going to focus on the economy,’” said one Democratic strategist, granted anonymity to speak candidly about party strategy. “‘I’m not a crazy Democrat.’”

The Democrats’ focus on normality in part reflects a party that believes that the first two years of Trump’s second term have generated such an electoral backlash that they need to do only the bare minimum to take advantage. The president has seen his approval rating sink to new lows in recent months, hindered by a growing sense his administration hasn’t delivered on the promises he made during the 2024 campaign.

But the strategy might also reflect a party tacitly acknowledging that — to some degree — it had lost sight of the political basics, running candidates so overstuffed with poll-tested soundbites and activist-driven demands that they were unable to connect with average voters.

“If we have a political strategy of coming across as normal, we might have bigger problems,” said Dembo, the party’s nominee in Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District. “Hopefully, you’re just a normal dude and don’t have to use it as a political ploy.”

Dembo, a former Navy JAG and federal prosecutor, talks about his career in public service and rejects comparisons to national Democrats, saying he prefers to emulate Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear. (Beshear won the 6th District when he ran for re-election in 2023.)
MI House Races (7854x5235, AR: 1.50)Republicans fiercely dispute that Democrats have recruited candidates who come across as normal and argue that even if they had, the larger party’s lurch to the left in this year’s primaries has convinced most moderate voters that the party is now controlled by extremists.

Indeed, much of the GOP’s messaging this year has focused on labeling Democrats as extremists, “perverts” or “communists,” efforts they say are aimed at broadly disqualifying Democratic candidates for all but the most liberal of voters.

“If Democrats wanted to run ‘normal’ candidates, they probably should've nominated some,” said Mike Marinella, spokesperson for the National Republican Congressional Committee.

Some Democratic candidates have helped Republicans make the case that the broader party still holds fringe views, comments that GOP strategists say they’ll use against the larger Democratic Party. Democratic candidates like Manny Rutinel in Colorado’s 8th District, Randy Villegas in California’s 22nd District, William Lawrence in Michigan’s 7th District and Colin Dunlap in Maine’s 2nd District also advanced in the primaries of key races over the opposition of some Democrats in Washington.

The backdrop for Democrats’ normalcy push is a spate of polls showing that many voters who disapprove of Trump aren’t yet ready to vote for a Democrat.

That slim but significant group is captured in generic ballot surveys, which show Democrats leading Republicans by about 6.5 percentage points, according to an average of polls compiled by the Silver Bulletin. That’s a much smaller gap than the difference between voters who approve and disapprove of the president: The Silver Bulletin’s polling average finds about 58% of voters disapprove of Trump, compared to about 38% who approve.

If Democratic candidates can win over more of the Trump disapprovers, party strategists say, it could turn a good midterm election into a great one, in which the party wins majorities in Congress by comfortable margins.

Democratic candidates interviewed by NOTUS said they meet voters who fit this category all the time.

“I mean, they’re kind of the name of the game,” said Bobby Pulido, a Democrat running for a House seat in Texas. “The people are not happy right now.”

Pulido, a famous Tejano musician, began playing quinceaneras in the state’s 15th District this year after responding to a criticism from his Republican opponent, Monica de la Cruz. It’s part of an effort to “speak the same language” as this Hispanic-heavy, rural area while being himself.
Bobby Pulido (4900x3267, AR: 1.50)“I’m not a city boy. I don’t dress in penny loafers,” he said, adding that he was just trying to "dispel the notion of what they think a Democrat is.”

“Hey, I just want you to have more affordable health care and try to make life better for you.”

Republicans have countered by pointing to Pulido’s own controversial history. But he’s one of many Democrats running for Congress emphasizing how their personal lives resemble those of the voters they’re trying to win.

Bennett, a onetime helicopter pilot in the Navy running in New Jersey’s 7th District, told NOTUS that she talks about the exorbitant cost of child care she faces for her children, or how she’s stopped eating beef because of rising prices.

“These are not talking points,” Bennett said. “This is my life.”

Dembo talks about how his family members are farmers. And Molder, a mayor in Tennessee’s 5th District, said he’s attended the same church since he was a child, proof that he’s a member of the community even if he’s also a member of a political party that most in the district don’t support.

“People I speak with aren’t necessarily looking for permission to become Democrats,” Molder said. “They’re looking for permission to vote for one.”

Democratic strategists think the strategy is already showing signs of paying off. They point to a series of internal party polls that show Democrats like Dembo and Pulido performing better than the generic ballot would suggest. The image of the average Democrat is so abysmally low in the minds of most voters, party operatives say privately, that it’s relatively easy to surpass their expectations with merely competent candidates.
Rebecca Bennett,Alex Hydrean,Rosie Bennett,Millie Bennett (6156x4104, AR: 1.50)No serious candidate has ever pledged to run an abnormal campaign that demonstrates how little in common he or she has with voters. And dating back to Trump’s first election in 2016, Democratic candidates have emphasized the need to prioritize “kitchen table” issues over other subjects. Joe Biden, in fact, premised his entire presidential campaign in 2020 in part on a return to normalcy.

But an approach that seems easy and commonsense in the abstract can suddenly become much harder in practice, say political veterans.

“When you’re in politics, there’s a lot of forces moving you,” said Max Rose, a former Democratic lawmaker from New York who lost his re-election bid in 2020. “There’s constituents, there’s family, there’s social media, there’s leadership, all types of things in your head. It’s a lot of input. It’s a lot of data.

“It’s hard to push all that aside and say, ‘Hey man, your shit costs too much, and I’m going to make it cheaper,’” he said.

The strongest force influencing Democrats might be Trump himself, thanks to relentless comments and actions that the party’s candidates can’t help but react to. But part of being normal, Democrats say, is focusing more on making life easier for people than opposing the president.

“If I’m spending time worrying about the ballroom and not the trade practices that are killing our farm economy, then I’m not representing,” McDonald Rivet said. “I’m just getting myself on social media.

“For the most part,” she said, “when I hear people talk about Democrats, they think we are more interested in damaging Donald Trump than bringing prices down.”
MI House Races (8049x5366, AR: 1.50)The congresswoman said members of her party don’t always keep the focus where it needs to be.

“Every once in a while, I talk to a member of the caucus who will say things to me, like, ‘As soon as we get the majority, we have to impeach the president,’” she said. “And I look at them and I say, ‘I won’t come back if they do that.’”

Republicans had considered McDonald Rivet’s seat in Michigan’s 8th Congressional District as a clear opportunity, though their hopes appeared to suffer a setback last week after a candidate who dropped out of the race, Thomas Smith, unexpectedly won the party’s primary over a Trump-endorsed candidate.

Democrats consider the plainspoken McDonald Rivet one of their most entrenched incumbents, thanks in part to her normalcy and message discipline. But even she can occasionally stray from her own advice in the face of Trump’s actions: In an interview, she called Trump an “idiot” because of the way he posted on social media.

“Please don’t use that I just called the president an ‘idiot,’” she said. “So sorry for doing that.”
entries.author: Alex Roarty

entries.title: From 2 a.m. Wakeups to Two-Hour Drives, Commanders Fans Are Committed to Camp
entries.summary: Hundreds of fans braved the summer heat to show up early for Saturday’s training camp practice.
entries.content:
It was one of those mornings where you know it’s going to be really hot outside. The sun had not yet risen on Saturday, but the rising temperature and heavy humidity were foreboding.

And yet the three parking lots outside the Commanders practice facility in Ashburn featured a line of people so long it started to weave around the gravel lot.

These fans woke up at ungodly hours and some had driven more than 100 miles from all corners of the D.C. area, not to attend a game or even a scrimmage. They came for practice.

The NFL season is still over a month away but Commanders fans are already in regular season mode. On Saturday, they had their jerseys from all three eras of the franchise: Redskins, Football Team and Commanders. Some had handmade signs. Others showed up to Ashburn in full pads and helmets.

And while it’s easy to call these people crazy for doing all of this for a team that’s won three playoff games since 2000, there’s something endearing about what true love and fandom really look like.

“I cried as a kid when we used to lose, and now [it’s] joy,” said Antonio Cummings, who woke up at 4 a.m. to make the hourlong trek from Prince George’s County. “And I'm looking forward to a better year like we had in 2024. … I just want to support the guys. That's why I'm here early.”

VIDEO HERE

This year, the Commanders opened 11 training camp practices for fans to come watch. Seats and standing-room-only sections are on a first-come, first-served basis, which makes space particularly competitive on days when more than 3,000 people show up. So if you want the best view of linebacker Odafe Oweh stretching or quarterback Jayden Daniels whipping a football with a towel or new receiver Stefon Diggs running a route, you’d best get to the facility early. Doors don’t open until about 7:30 a.m. for the 8:30 practices, but some fans start lining up before 6.

Josh and Logan May live two hours away from Ashburn in Greene County, Virginia, right outside of Charlottesville. They woke up at 3 a.m. and were on the road by 3:45 with their two young children. They were the first in line, at about 5:45.

“They actually get up pretty good for this,” Josh May said about their kids. “It's not like school.”

Rita Spong also lives about two hours away in Baltimore County, though she woke up a little earlier. “I got up at 2,” she said. That’s early, but nothing a little caffeine can’t fix.

“It was crazy, but then I got my coffee and I was lit the whole way,” Spong said, wearing a Daniels jersey shirt and holding a “WELCOME HOME DIGGS” sign.

Fans schlep out to Loudoun County for a multitude of reasons. Some want to see their favorite players. Others want visual proof of the improvements the team has made since last season’s disastrous 5-12 campaign. A select few are here mainly because tickets are free. But most of all, people come out of a deep love for this team — their team.

Montrell Pointer of Laurel, Maryland, got his dad to bring him because he dreams of playing in the NFL one day and wanted to see his favorite player, Terry McLaurin, in person.

“I love the Commanders,” Montrell said, wearing a black McLaurin jersey. “And I'm just trying to get some autographs and see them practice and see how they do and learn some stuff maybe.”

Waking up before dawn on the weekend to drive upwards of two hours to stand in line for more hours to watch NFL players practice in the searing sun and suffocating humidity for even more hours sounds like sane behavior to football fans. But to many others, it sounds like willingly jumping out of an airplane.

Friends and family might understand attending training camp, but they draw the line at hitting the road before the birds sing.

“One of my friends is actually coming here, and she's coming at 8 a.m., and I told her she was crazy,” said Mia Ovando, who lives about 10 minutes away from camp in Sterling.

Josh May’s mother loves Washington great Darrell Green and would do anything to see the Hall of Famer, who now works for the team, in person. But “when we told her what time we was coming, she said, ‘I think I'll miss it,’” he said.

For many fans, training camp is more than just a practice. It’s family time or a bonding experience. It’s a chance to pass down traditions and create a love that — unlike some friendships or even marriages — can overcome pain and sorrow and loss.

Nicandra Brown’s 81-year-old uncle is the reason she became a Commanders fan as a kid. Saturday was Kids Day at training camp and she and a friend brought their grandsons.

“This is our team,” Brown said. “We're trying to make sure they want to be Commander fans, too.”

Spong’s family was always “screaming and mad” when watching Commanders games, so she learned to scream and be mad, too. Especially when Washington loses.

“If we don't win, the whole week be just messed up for real,” she said. “Don't nobody better not say nothing to me on my job, like for real. Don't play. We serious about this. Like they don't understand. They don't understand.”

Many of the fans in line were bullish about the coming season. There was a near-consensus that Washington will reach the NFC championship game, as it did in 2024. And the recent signing of Diggs, a DMV native, received unanimous approval.

Afternoon temperatures were projected to be in the low 90s, with humidity making it feel closer to 100 degrees. But nobody in the early-morning crowd seemed deterred. Spong had a portable neck fan wrapped around her, sitting comfortably under her locs.

“I was proactive,” Spong said. “Got to thank Amazon. Got my little fan, so I'm ready.”

When asked about weathering the heat in his authentic Sean Taylor jersey, black track pants and gold Mr. T-esque oversized “W” chain, Cummings launched into an emphatic speech about how possibly risking heat exhaustion will contribute to the success of the Commanders this season.

“Listen, in order to be the best, you got to beat the best, and sometimes that means you got to stand in the kitchen,” Cummings began. “So I got to stand in the kitchen with the guys. You know, we got to cook up, whether it's in the heat, whether it's in the cold. We got to cook up. If it was 20 degrees, I'd be out here. So I sweat with them, too.”
entries.author: Martenzie Johnson

entries.title: Iran-U.S. Diplomacy Is Not Dead, but It Needs a Reset
entries.summary: Iran's reiteration of broad demands points to the need for a more comprehensive deal to begin resolving the war than U.S. officials had claimed.
entries.content:
Announcements from Iranian officials over the weekend quashed optimism that the U.S. and Iran are near a deal to end President Donald Trump’s war. The Iranian move to emphasize a broad set of demands suggested a need for more sophisticated diplomacy and bolstered fears that a compromise may be out of the Trump administration’s reach.

Optimistic Washington officials had pointed to talks between Iran and Oman, an Arab state aligned with the U.S. The two nations border the lynchpin of the Strait of Hormuz, the waterway along Iran’s southern border, where Iranian forces have disrupted traffic since Trump’s assault began, treating Hormuz as a strategic asset.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Vice President JD Vance have said the administration is now focused on increasing the flow of oil and gas through the strait to combat global price increases, not on the the broad goals Trump specified in initiating the conflict. The talks between Oman and Iran aim to cement a new understanding for ships to safely traverse the strait.

Those talks continue, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday. But their prospects are now more explicitly tied to a sweeping U.S.-Iran bargain.

The Iranian comments on Saturday, first coming from the country’s Supreme National Security Council and then emphasized by Araghchi, suggested Tehran will not agree to a limited deal about the strait without proof the U.S. is addressing broader Iranian demands. The declarations reiterated terms in a U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding Trump signed in June, including reparations for the war this year and for U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran in 2025, the withdrawal of the American blockade on Iranian ports and American troops around Iran, stopping attacks on Iran’s allies in the Middle East (notably Lebanon) and broad economic relief for Iranians from U.S. sanctions and asset freezes.

Officials familiar with the diplomacy and other experts told NOTUS that Iran’s latest comments suggest negotiations need a reset, with a U.S.-Iran settlement still feasible — and desirable for both parties — but harder to reach. The complications extend to the third parties serving as mediators: Oman, but also Saudi Arabia and other wealthy Gulf countries with deep ties to the Trump White House that view ending the war as an urgent security priority.

“Iran has long linked reopening Hormuz to reciprocal U.S. steps,” said Ali Vaez of the International Crisis Group think tank. He argued for the Trump administration to make a new step-by-step offer to partly meet Iran’s demands, rather than renewed American military pressure through further strikes, “which may satisfy Trump’s instincts but would only harden Tehran’s position.”

Opening with the U.S. assassination of Iran’s longtime supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, the war has fractured Iranian leadership. Hard-liners, for instance in the country’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, have expanded their influence in the policy-making establishment relative to figures more open to negotiations, and cited the war to emphasize wariness toward the U.S., a foe for many decades. Forces leery of engagement have ramped up criticism of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, and an IRGC commander gained a powerful post on the national security council on Sunday.

Sanam Vakil, an analyst at the Chatham House think tank, wrote on X that Iranian hardliners worry that too soft a deal with Trump would give him “an off ramp” to rebuild military power ahead of another campaign against Iran.

“Since Trump has proven himself, again and again, to be an unreliable negotiator, Tehran will not give away its most potent leverage unless and until the U.S. delivers on its own obligations,” Vaez told NOTUS, saying Iranian officials are being maximalist rhetorically but could eventually settle.

Iran knows the U.S. will never pay reparations, he added, “but Tehran demands it in order to secure as much sanctions relief as possible.”

Iran’s expectations suggest the country is unlikely to reach for what the U.S. presents as a quick and easy deal. That leaves Trump and others — like regional governments — to suggest a mutually agreeable path.

Trump told Axios on Sunday he is “low-keying it” and suggested Iran is feeling greater economic pain from the war than Americans. The president has told aides he is ready to declare victory and abandon previously stated goals of the war, like a new limit on Iranian nuclear capacity, The Wall Street Journal reported. Both outlets suggested he is unlikely to restart military strikes in response to Iran’s new demands.

Saudi Arabia has discouraged saber-rattling by Trump, with a Middle Eastern official telling NOTUS that urging from the country has “been extremely helpful” in supplementing the Oman-Iran talks. The official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because of the delicate nature of the negotiations, said the Saudis were “freaking out” about being targeted by Iranian allies in Iraq and Yemen.

That official noted, however, that Israel remains a wild card. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu helped initiate the war and continues to direct Israeli attacks in Lebanon, which could anger Iran. The offensive there “is a huge card [Israel] can play with,” said the official, who also argued pro-Israel donors in the U.S. could nudge Trump and Republicans away from diplomacy. GOP lawmakers have already suggested they could stymie U.S steps to cool tensions with Iran.

People familiar with the U.S. administration’s thinking have also told NOTUS that Trump is extremely unwilling to appear to be capitulating to Iran and is continuously enthusiastic about revisiting military options.

Saudi and other regional officials are frustrated with the sense Iran is delaying peace, but they are also struggling to secure a commitment for a de-escalation from Washington.

They see Vance, who has expressed doubts about the war and Israel’s influence in U.S. politics, as an ally, yet acknowledge Trump’s volatility remains the key factor in negotiations.

Randa Slim, of the Stimson Center think tank, said Middle Eastern leaders don’t view Vance as having the final word in negotiations, but they “trust him more than [Secretary of State] Marco Rubio to listen to and convey their concerns.”

Rubio is a longtime Iran hawk and is seen as close to Netanyahu.

“Even as they see Iran is overplaying its hand,” Gulf Arab states generally agree “the war must end,” said Yasmine Farouk, also with Crisis Group. “Pending issues, like the permanent status of Hormuz, should be addressed by all other means, but not through a return to a full-scale war that threatens their infrastructure.”
entries.author: Akbar Shahid Ahmed

entries.title: Home Rule Meets Helmets
entries.content:
Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: A motorcycle bill, federal workers’ forced relocations and a setback for the Commanders. 





THE LATEST

Could helmet hair eventually be a thing of the past in D.C.?

In what one could call niche and targeted legislation, two Republican members of Congress have introduced a bill that would repeal D.C.’s law requiring that anyone riding a motorcycle wear a helmet.

One of the bill’s sponsors is Rep. Derrick Van Orden, a Wisconsin Republican known for riding his souped-up Harley Davidson around D.C. But Grace Kim, his spokesperson, tells NOTUS that the bill wasn’t written just so Van Orden could feel the wind on his head.

“The federal government has had a hand in helmet requirements going back to the Highway Safety Act, which used highway funding as leverage to get states to adopt helmet laws,” she wrote in an email. “That’s part of why D.C. is an important place to start. If Congress can change the policy here, it opens the door to having a larger conversation about the federal government’s role in helmet mandates across the country.”

D.C. being a testing ground for that policy change could irk plenty of residents. Recall that D.C. doesn’t have voting representation in Congress, and members of the House and Senate regularly weigh in on local matters without speaking directly to the people who would be most affected.

The bill’s passage could also create an inconsistent patchwork of helmet laws across the Washington region. Both Maryland and Virginia currently require that motorcyclists wear helmets.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, for its part, is clear: “If you're ever in a serious motorcycle crash, the best hope you have for protecting your brain is a motorcycle helmet.” The federal agency says that per vehicle miles traveled in 2024, motorcyclists were almost 27 times more likely than car occupants to die in crashes and five times more likely to be injured.

The American Motorcyclist Association says that helmet use shouldn’t be mandated and that “helmet use alone is insufficient to ensure a motorcyclist’s safety.”

On the Senate side, the bill is being sponsored by Sen. Tim Sheehy, a Republican from Montana — which has a population density of 7.8 people per square mile, compared to D.C.’s 11,489.





DEEP DIVE

A plan to relocate 17 Interior Department employees from Reston to D.C. later this month has irked a pair of Virginia’s representatives, who call the move a disguised forced resignation.

“We have serious concerns about this. I think this is going to amount to all the employees being fired or leaving government because there's not enough room in the D.C. offices for all the staff to be relocated,” Democratic Rep. Suhas Subramanyam told NOTUS. “It’s going to increase costs and time for people when it comes to their commute.”

It’s the latest example of the Trump administration asking federal workers to relocate. In June, Interior asked 600 employees to make the same move from Reston. Virginia Reps. Subramanyam and James Walkinshaw, also a Democrat, wrote a letter last week to Secretary Doug Burgum asking for the agency’s rationale.

“This administration, from the very beginning, wanted to traumatize federal workers. They said it themselves. So here we are. They're going to continue to try these agency moves, and we're going to continue to fight them,” Subramanyam said. “We plan to use our authority in Congress, if we're the majority next year, to fight all of these relocations.”





FROM THE DISTRICT

D.C. 1, DOJ 0. A federal judge has shot down the Department of Justice’s attempt to force D.C. to turn over an unredacted copy of its voter registration list, NOTUS’ Martin Austermuhle reports. The Trump administration has been trying for a year to gain access to the voter rolls of almost every state, but has now lost 21 of the 30 legal battles it has started. Trump officials say they want to ensure states are properly maintaining their voter lists, but critics say they are trying to unduly interfere in elections.

The District’s luxury housing market is booming. Tech and finance executives are snapping up “trophy homes” in the city, The Wall Street Journal reports, causing D.C.’s luxury home inventory to fall 22% by the end of this year’s first quarter.

Cheers to (Ira and) the Governor. Ira Johnson and his French bulldog, Rocco — better known as “The Governor” — cruise down 14th Street Northwest for community, but their online content has won them hundreds of thousands of followers, The Washington Post reports.





FROM MARYLAND

Dam! In the past two weeks, two people have been attacked by rabid beavers in Frederick County’s Cunningham Falls State Park, Axios DC reports.Officials say it’s not a larger trend.





FROM YOUR FEED

Claude Instagram (956x1190, AR: 0.80)D.C. residents use Anthropic’s Claude AI more than anywhere else in the U.S. “by a wide margin,” the company posted on Instagram last week.

But it’s not that local tech bros and policy wonks are out-prompting those in a city like San Francisco. Rather, the map represents a per capita count, propelling D.C. above many states.

Even if the comparison were apples to apples, we wouldn’t trust this map. The state placements are questionable and, worst of all, it’s missing Maine!





D.C. TRIVIA


How many U.S. presidents are buried within D.C.’s city limits?

  1. None
  2. One
  3. Three
Email us the answer — the first reader who gets it right gets a shout-out. The answer will be at the end of the newsletter tomorrow.





SPORTS

Commanders training camp is nothing more than a glorified practice, but that doesn’t stop some fans from making a serious commitment to attend. NOTUS’ Martenzie Johnson joined some of the very first people in line at Saturday’s session, hearing about their early wake-up times and lengthy commutes. One fan from Baltimore County said she got up at 2 a.m. to make the trek.

“It was crazy,” she said, holding a sign she made for new receiver Stefon Diggs. “But then I got my coffee and I was lit the whole way.”

In less endearing news, the team faced its first real setback of the season Saturday afternoon when linchpin left tackle Laremy Tunsil went down with what has been reported as a torn triceps. While the team hasn’t confirmed the injury, the All-Pro lineman is expected to miss several months. Martenzie writes that Washington could turn to a young player like Brandon Coleman to fill the void, or look outside of the organization for a suitable replacement.





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@notus.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson.

entries.title: Trump and the Supremes
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Trump v. the courts. What the Senate left undone from its to-do list. RIP Beth (the vacuum). Purple-area Democrats’ plan. Rep. Case survives a deeper blue wave in Hawaii. Rep. Miller vows to stay put. Time to reset negotiations with Iran? And: Why trust in rural doctors is effective against medical conspiracies.

THE LATEST

Trump thumbs his nose at the Supremes? Early in Trump 2.0, there was a great deal of consternation around the idea that Donald Trump might directly ignore court rulings — including those from the Supreme Court. (These were not baseless worries; JD Vance specifically called for taking an Andrew Jackson approach to high court rulings the White House didn’t like in the administration’s second month.)

In practice, while federal judges have at times been outraged at what they have called open defiance of their rulings, the general consensus during Trump’s second term is that federal courts have successfully checked presidential power on numerous occasions.

This week opens a new conversation about obeying the spirit of rulings versus the letter of them. In June, the Supreme Court ruled against the president in upholding birthright citizenship and protecting the independence of the Fed. Then last week, the administration rolled out new executive orders limiting birthright citizenship’s reach, along with a new effort to fire Fed board of governors member Lisa Cook. Whether you see these moves as court defiance or reasonable responses to court orders depends on your point of view. Either way, they will more than likely end up back before SCOTUS at some point.

Keep an eye on this, from NOTUS’ Eric Katz: A federal judge ruled Friday that the Department of Veterans Affairs cannot cancel the existing contract with its union, as it had planned. When asked by NOTUS whether the VA would comply with the order, a spokesperson said he could not comment. Asked again whether the VA would honor the injunction, the spokesperson did not respond.

Mike Davis, a staunch Trump ally and founder of judicial advocacy group Article III Project who has advocated for the White House to ignore some lower court rulings, told NOTUS’ Jasmine Wright that the Trump administration is just exercising its available options.

“The Supreme Court issued rulings,” Davis said, “and now the Trump administration should do the necessary follow-up legal work, including stopping the Chinese birth tourism industry and providing Lisa Cook notice and opportunity to respond.”

Open tabs: Trump names Will Scharf as White House counsel (Reuters); Trump to Axios: "We are low keying it" with Iran (Axios); Israel Rejects Next Phase of Trump’s Gaza Peace Plan (WSJ); Ocasio-Cortez Says She Is Freezing Her Eggs and Still Mulling a Presidential Run (NYT)

From the Hill


The Senate powers through. Wow, these folks can really get moving when they wanna go on recess, huh? In the wee hours of Saturday morning, the Senate confirmed Todd Blanche as attorney general and passed its version of a stopgap spending bill that ensures there will be no government shutdown before the midterms — as long as the House agrees.

What the Senate didn’t do: Pass a college sports bill (despite Trump’s urging) or cryptocurrency legislation. It also punted a Republican budget bill aimed at kick-starting money for new voter ID requirements and the Iran war.

The actual most important Senate news: Beth, Sen. Chuck Grassley’s long-serving vacuum, succumbed to old age over the weekend. She had devoted her life to cleanliness. RIP.

From the campaign trail


Normiemaxxing matters: Purple-area Democrats hope to win over the voters who don’t like Trump and don’t like Democrats — the so-called double-haters Trump won in 2024. They can’t do that if they’re seen as weirdos, NOTUS’ Alex Roarty reports. “The most important communication aspect of this is, ‘Hey, I’m a normal human being who’s going to focus on the economy. I’m not a crazy Democrat,’” is how one Democratic strategist explained the game plan for swing-district Democrats running at a time when a left-wing surge is dominating the national headlines.

The response to this plan kinda writes itself, as you’d imagine. “If Democrats wanted to run ‘normal’ candidates, they probably should've nominated some,” an NRCC spokesperson said.

Hawaii’s survivor: Democratic Rep. Ed Case beat back a challenge from progressive state Sen. Jarrett Keohokalole on Saturday, breaking a streak of Democratic incumbents losing to primary challengers on their left. Case grabbed 56% of the vote to Keohokalole’s 36%.

Miller stays in: Republican Rep. Max Miller is vowing to stay in his fight for reelection, his spokesperson confirmed to The New York Times despite calls for him to resign over allegations of physically abusing his ex-wife and daughter. Miller would’ve had to withdraw by Saturday to allow party leaders to choose a replacement on the ballot by today.

From the White House


It’s time to reset negotiations with Iran while a settlement is still feasible — and desirable for both parties — but notably harder to reach, experts and officials familiar with the diplomacy told NOTUS’ Akbar Shahid Ahmed. With Iran’s reiteration this weekend of broad demands despite American military pressure, negotiating an end to the war has proved difficult for U.S. allies in the region trying to secure a commitment for a de-escalation in Washington. Trump doesn’t want to look like he’s giving in to Iran’s demands and remains continuously enthusiastic about revisiting military options, people familiar with the U.S. administration’s thinking told Akbar.

“Since Trump has proven himself, again and again, to be an unreliable negotiator, Tehran will not give away its most potent leverage unless and until the U.S. delivers on its own obligations,” said Ali Vaez of the International Crisis Group think tank.

NOTUS METRO

Sign up for our local newsletter, written by Martin Austermuhle and Zara Norman.

Local news: D.C. Wins Fight Against Trump Administration Over Voter Rolls, by Martin Austermuhle

Sports desk: Laremy Tunsil’s Injury Deals a Major Blow to the Commanders’ Offense, by Martenzie Johnson

NEW ON NOTUS

A rural doctor vs. the conspiracies. West Virginia remains one of the most-vaccinated states in the nation; recent surveys show majorities of the population still support the strict vaccination requirements required to attend public schools in the state. NOTUS’ Margaret Manto dives into the why and finds trust between patients and generational, small-practice doctors like Mark Tomsho in Summersville.

Why this doctor is so effective: Connection. “People know you, and they know that you’ve extended yourself into the community, and you’ve been there and your practice has been there, both for their well-child visits and when their children are ill. They tend to trust you,” Tomsho told Margaret.

The future is moving away from this kind of medicine. Small private practices are closing at a rapid rate, and the large medical groups that replace them have created a facelessness to medicine that local public health officials say could break the trust doctors like Tomsho have built up. He’s 70 years old, and it’s not clear his kind of practice can be replicated.

These doctors have left a legacy of a belief in medical guidance. But those rules are encountering the same rising national distrust of public health that has led immunization rates to fall in many other places.

The question: Can West Virginia’s herd immunity against vaccine conspiracies survive the shift to Big Medicine?

More: Joe Biden’s Cancer Has Spread Further Into His Body, His Son Says, by Angie Orellana Hernandez

Abdul El-Sayed Calls Streamer Hasan Piker’s Past 9/11 Comment ‘Dumb,’ by Jenna Monnin

entries.title: An Antidote to the Anti-Vaccine Movement Lives in Rural West Virginia
entries.summary: Growing distrust in the medical establishment is spelling trouble for public health. An answer may be in the very kind of care that’s growing more obsolete.
entries.content:
This story was published with the assistance of the Journalism & Women Symposium (JAWS) Health Journalism Fellowship, supported by The Commonwealth Fund.

For a pediatrician, Mark Tomsho is surprisingly calm when talking about the decline of childhood vaccination rates.

“Pendulums swing, pendulums swing,” he mused, Zen-like, in his office between seeing patients one April evening. “Nothing stays the same. And I find that truth and reality usually win out.”

Tomsho has spent the last 40 years practicing medicine in the small town of Summersville, West Virginia, population less than 5,000. Nestled in the rolling hills of Nicholas County, Summersville has voted for President Donald Trump three times. It has an annual potato festival. It’s best known for coal mining and the large, man-made lake ringed with white cliffs that poaches tourists from New River Gorge National Park, a 30 minutes’ drive south.

It’s also known for its high vaccination rates. Local health officials credit Tomsho for that.

“I have seen the difference in cervical cancer rates based on who the health care provider was, because I know they were vaccinated if they saw Mark,” said Anita Stewart, health officer of the Nicholas County Health Department and a practicing OB-GYN.

West Virginia has some of the highest childhood vaccine rates of any state in the U.S., and Nicholas County routinely rivals the more populous counties that surround it in the number of vaccines distributed.

That all feels under threat now. A national movement pushing distrust in the medical establishment has ascended to the highest echelons of public health. Historic measles outbreaks have cropped up in unvaccinated communities. And the local figures like Tomsho who have long served as the backstop to that kind of pervasive politics are dwindling in numbers.

The pendulum is swinging.

Small private practices are closing at a rapid rate, making way for big hospital groups that can afford to be in rural areas like Summersville. That shift has had to happen to maintain health coverage in the often forgotten parts of the country. But it's also created a facelessness to medicine that many fear could undercut the herd immunity doctors have worked for decades to establish in their hometowns.

Without established relationships with doctors, patients are more likely to believe misinformation.

In a KFF poll, nearly 40% of people who didn’t have a trusted health care provider said they believed it is “definitely” or “probably” true that the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine causes autism in children, a claim that isn’t backed up by scientific evidence. When people did have a trusted provider, that percentage dropped to about 25%.

“People know you, and they know that you’ve extended yourself into the community, and you’ve been there and your practice has been there, both for their well-child visits and when their children are ill. They tend to trust you,” Tomsho said.
Tomsho-21 copy.jpg (2149x1432, AR: 1.50)Tomsho is soft-spoken and bespectacled, with close-cropped white hair and a more-than-passing resemblance to Anthony Fauci. His desk and office are as full and busy as his schedule; on the ground, piles of papers and medical files sit beside two framed diplomas that are unlikely, from the looks of it, to ever find a home on the wall.

“A name everyone in the county knows,” one father said of Tomsho while sitting next to his son in the waiting room. Rainbow letters above read, “The Future of the World is in This Room.”

Tomsho has practiced medicine in Summersville since July 1986. He’s treated families for generations, watching them grow and shrink. Some families said they drove more than 45 minutes to see him that day.

“Trust helps them to agree with what we recommend,” Tomsho continued. “As corporate medicine takes over, I think we’ll see less of that.”

***

Across the street from Tomsho’s office is a regional hospital where he, until recently, had admitting privileges so he could follow his young patients there if necessary. He had to stop due to health issues of his own.

The state’s largest health system, WVU Medicine, purchased the hospital in 2018.
Tomsho-27 copy.jpg (2500x1667, AR: 1.50)The hospital is a physical reminder that Tomsho, who is 70 and reluctantly considering retirement — it “crosses my wife’s mind a lot” — is a vestige of a waning kind of health care.

Tomsho’s practice doesn’t have a website; he is elusive via email. His waiting room feels almost quaint in an age where doctors are Amazon employees and AI agents. An intermittent beeping noise, like one from an AOL dial-up modem, constantly emits from behind the check-in desk.

That’s our fax machine, the receptionist tells a young parent confused by the noise. It’s “either trying to receive or send a fax.”

For a long time, West Virginia’s approach to rural health looked more like Tomsho’s office than not. In the 1800s, the state opened three local hospitals to treat miners and other industrial workers — “not something that you're going to see in other states” at that time, said Katie Thompson, a historian at the William A. Neal Museum of the Health Sciences at West Virginia University.
Tomsho-2 copy.jpg (2434x1622, AR: 1.50)“Things in West Virginia are very community based,” Thompson said. “A lot of the health care is set up in West Virginia with access in mind.”

West Virginia was one of the first states to offer community polio vaccination events in the 1950s, and doctors in the state were still doing house calls even into the 1960s, long after that practice was discontinued elsewhere.

The state passed a no-exceptions school vaccine requirement in 1937. It took until 1980 for all 50 states to pass vaccination mandates for school children. West Virginia is the only state that has, since the inception of vaccine mandates, always required all of its public school students to receive all of their shots.

The strengths of such a system were on display during the rollout of the COVID-19 vaccine, when West Virginia outpaced other states in how quickly it distributed its allocated shots.

Unlike other states, West Virginia declined to distribute the vaccine through pharmacy chains like Walgreens and CVS. Instead, it created its own network of local, independently-owned pharmacies and long-term care facilities to distribute the vaccine. The National Guard helped.

“There’s nothing like being able to help your neighbor,” one local pharmacy owner told NBC News at the time.

Like elsewhere in the country, West Virginia has faced attempts to change its pro-vaccination policies. Gov. Patrick Morrisey is a staunch Robert F. Kennedy Jr. ally who’s pushed to align his state with the vaccine-skeptical Make America Healthy Again movement. He’s tried to weaken the state’s childhood vaccine mandates.

Public health officials say they’re fielding more questions from West Virginians about vaccines and diseases, like measles, hepatitis B and RSV.

“I think it’s certainly highlighted the importance of listening to patients and community members and others about the questions that they have related to immunization, and being able to answer them,” said Elaine Darling, who co-runs The Center for Rural Health Development.

As of spring 2026, the majority of West Virginians supported vaccines and vaccination requirements for school-aged children.

“West Virginians have a tendency to try to protect each other,” Darling said. “I think that probably does factor in quite a bit to why we're able to maintain high vaccination rates.”

Still, the state isn’t immune to the financial challenges of maintaining a localized rural health system. A report last year found that of West Virginia’s 33 rural hospitals, 13 are in danger of closing; five could close in the next two to three years.

WVU Medicine and Vandalia Health System now own 70% of the hospitals across the state, according to the West Virginia Center on Budget and Policy.
Tomsho-28 copy.jpg (1982x1322, AR: 1.50)The change has happened rapidly. Three health systems merged to form Vandalia in 2022 and 2023. WVU Medicine has doubled the number of hospitals it owns over the last four years.

In some respects, these health giants have saved struggling rural hospitals from the brink of closure. When WVU Medicine announced that it would take over the operations of the medical center in Fairmont, a town close to Morgantown, where West Virginia University is located, and reopen it while it built a new, 100-bed hospital next door, the community was happy.

“That’s a pretty big deal for people who need care in that area,” Thompson said. “I haven’t heard a lot of negative.”

But that change comes with a cost. New health providers can mean new faces, new systems and new challenges with insurance.

“That erodes the long-term trust,” Tomsho said.

***
Study after study have reached the same conclusion: The more time people spend with their doctors, the more they know them, and feel known, the more they trust the system.

Big health systems don’t always work that way. More advanced scheduling systems limit providers’ down time and result in shorter visits with patients. There’s less time to learn about their lives and build a relationship with them.

At smaller practices in more rural areas, doctors are “known as community members,” said Richard Frankel, who studies clinician-patient relationships at the Indiana University School of Medicine. “They know their patients’ families.”

“In larger communities, it’s much more anonymous, and there may well be a feeling on the patient’s part of being just a cog in a wheel,” he said.

“It’s like showing up at church and suddenly there’s a different preacher,” said Mark Hall, a professor emeritus at Wake Forest University who’s studied patient-provider relationships and health care consolidation. “It doesn’t matter that they’re a perfectly good preacher. ‘Wait, where’s my preacher?’”

A 2020 study in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, found that patients saw big hospital groups as “less navigable, accountable, and transparent to outsiders” — even if they also recognized that they needed these big health systems to come in and save their health institutions. They were “mostly beneficial for the long-term viability.”

***

When Tomsho first arrived in Summersville, his new neighbors weren’t so sure he’d last.

“‘Are you just going to be here a year or two and then leave like everybody else?’” he recounted being asked.

Tomsho grew up in California, started his pediatrics residency in Colorado, then transferred to Pittsburgh when his mother got sick. He came to Summersville as part of the National Health Service Corps, a program that sends doctors to rural, underserved areas. He joined because it “aligned with his ethics” and helped pay for medical school.

“I came here, visited. There was no pediatrician. So I said, ‘This is just what I want to do,’” Tomsho said. “I was starting out just fresh, and I was still young and enthusiastic.”

Tomsho-3 copy.jpg (2296x1531, AR: 1.50)Tomsho-32 copy.jpg (2500x1667, AR: 1.50)It’s easy to see why Summersville would entice a young doctor: It’s in a beautiful area, and the people are friendly. Every fall, the Army Corps of Engineers releases millions of gallons of water from Summersville Lake into the Gauley River; the ensuing “Gauley Season” of temporary whitewater rapids draws rafters from across the country. The town is quiet the rest of the year.

It was just him, a nurse and a receptionist at first. They set up in a “little tin building” that now serves as the town’s pharmacy. The original “Top Gun” was in theaters.

Tomsho had to prove himself. He wrote a column in the newspaper for a while, which helped. Word of mouth did, too. He’s given talks at the local schools and participated in local health fairs, sports physical clinics. At some point it became clear that he wasn’t going anywhere. In 2022, he was even chosen to serve as the 52nd grand marshal of the Nicholas County Potato Festival.

***

Forty years after Tomsho first started practicing medicine, West Virginia is still a place that draws a certain kind of person. A certain kind of doctor.

Kara Piechowski, a clinical pharmacist and recently-graduated physician from West Virginia, took a personal interest in the state’s vaccine policy when Morrisey pushed legislation to weaken it in 2025.

“I created a website, just a personal Google website, and coded it to where I could put all of our West Virginia legislators’ emails in one link, and then did a draft email that you could tailor,” Piechowski said. “And that link was used, like, 7,500 times to contact our state legislators.”

Piechowski said she plans to return to the state after she completes her residency. (She recently matched into a combined internal medicine and pediatrics residency program at the Ohio State University.)

The trust providers form with patients in West Virginia is “unmatched” compared to the other states where she’s worked, Piechowski said.

“You just don’t get to know patients on a level that you do here in West Virginia in a lot of, if not most, other places,” she said. “I think people say, or think at least, ‘This is someone who’s like me and has my best interests at heart, so maybe I’ll trust them.’ But that’s just a guess.”
Tomsho-24 copy.jpg (2403x1602, AR: 1.50)When asked what he’d do if West Virginia stopped requiring vaccines for public school attendance, Tomsho remained characteristically calm.

“We’ll just have to do as much of an in-office campaign, maybe a little bit in local media, about the importance of vaccines and our experience with prevention of these vaccine-preventable diseases,” he said.

Tomsho shrugs off suggestions that he personally has some kind of especially effective approach to getting people vaccinated. It’s just how it is in West Virginia. The American Academy of Pediatrics is very strong in the state, he said, and they encourage it. There’s a nonprofit rural health network that focuses on vaccinations. The insurance companies still encourage it, and Medicaid still encourages it.

Pendulums swing, pendulums swing.

But he allowed that it might also have something to do with the fact that he is simply there.

“It’s their ability to decide that empowers them, and I think that’s important to them,” Tomsho said of his vaccine-hesitant families. “We do not exclude them from the practice in any way. I just tell them, ‘I will ask you about it every visit to make sure you haven’t changed your mind.’”

entries.title: RFK Jr. Proposes New Reporting Requirements for Ultra-Processed Foods
entries.summary: Manufacturers would be able to keep selling products under the proposed rule.
entries.content:
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has taken a swing against processed foods in the United States, but didn’t go as far as the food industry had feared.

Food manufacturers would have to submit information about additives, including dyes, preservatives, sweeteners and emulsifiers, to the Food and Drug Administration, according to a proposed rule detailed Monday by administration officials.

In a sigh of relief for the industry, the packaged foods would be able to remain on the shelves in the meantime.

Additives “generally recognized as safe,” or GRAS, currently fall under a regulatory loophole that allows them to be included in foods with little oversight. Kennedy and officials touted the proposal as a fulfillment of his promises to improve diet and nutrition in the United States, where people get more than half their calories from ultra-processed foods. For decades, the loophole has raised concerns among consumer and nutrition advocates.

“We cannot reverse America’s chronic disease epidemic without transforming our

food system,” Kennedy said in a statement. “These historic actions bring greater transparency to what’s in our food and stronger science to federal nutrition policy.”

Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas also said the agency has submitted for interagency review a definition of ultra-processed foods — which could inform new front-of-package labels Kennedy has promised.

Kennedy took the helm of HHS last year with ambitious promises to crack down on the ultra-processed food he, his “Make America Healthy Again” supporters and nutritionists blame for the nation’s epidemic of obesity and chronic disease.

The administration revamped the federal nutrition guidelines earlier this year and extracted promises from a handful of large food companies to remove certain dyes from their products. Last year, Kennedy directed the FDA to start working on GRAS reform.

The proposed rule isn’t final and will be available for public comment. For products with GRAS substances that are already on the market, the FDA would have 180 days to review information submitted by manufacturers. It would have 45 days to review applications for new GRAS ingredients. Officials said Congress would need to delegate them the authority to mandate GRAS review before products are on the market.

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region

The regulation would close “a decades-old information gap” and “improve transparency and the agency’s oversight of the U.S. food supply,” Diamantas said.

“Americans deserve confidence that the ingredients in their food are subject to transparent,

science-based oversight, and today’s actions strengthen both sides of that equation,” he said.

Thomas Gremillion, director of food policy at the Consumer Federation of America, said he’s glad to see the administration mandate notices of GRAS ingredients, calling it a “long overdue policy,” so the FDA can fully assess the safety of the nation’s food supply.

But he worries the FDA will end up rubber-stamping GRAS ingredients because it lacks the time and staffing to conduct a thorough review of so many ingredients.

“Nothing in this suggests that FDA will actually do anything to review the safety of the substances for which GRAS determinations have been made,” Gremillion said.

Former FDA Commissioner David Kessler said “the proposed GRAS actions do not tackle the root causes of chronic disease in this country.”

Kessler also told NOTUS the White House is holding up action on a petition he filed last August calling on the agency to legally strip refined carbohydrates like high fructose corn syrup from the U.S. food supply.

Kennedy’s “MAHA report” last year laying out his priorities promised to “fund independent studies evaluating the health impact of self-affirmed GRAS food ingredients, prioritizing risks to children and informing transparent FDA rulemaking.”

Lobbying on the pending regulations by trade associations, companies and organizations has skyrocketed in the past year, NOTUS has reported.

The food industry has rallied around draft legislation from Rep. Kat Cammack (R-Florida) that takes an even softer approach. It would retroactively approve ingredients currently considered GRAS and nullify state food-additive laws, which have surged this year amid food safety reform efforts by MAHA activists.

entries.title: The U.S. Spent $2.2 Billion on Immigration Detention Centers, With More to Go
entries.summary: CoreCivic and the Geo Group are finding it more lucrative to let the federal government be the landlord.
entries.content:
The Trump administration’s new strategy of purchasing privately owned detention centers has already flooded one company with cash, and it’s worrying immigration advocates that it will upend local oversight efforts.

Over the past two months, the Department of Homeland Security has purchased four lockups in California, Minnesota and Kansas totaling $2.2 billion from CoreCivic, one of two major players in the immigration detention industry.

The federal government is likely to take ownership of even more detention centers owned by CoreCivic and its main competitor, the Geo Group. The companies’ top executives highlighted their negotiations with the Trump administration for further sales during calls with investors Thursday.

While DHS becomes the landlord, the deals in July and August have so far allowed CoreCivic to get paid for day-to-day operations. This change in ownership maintains the status quo on the ground but could make it harder for local officials to oversee what is happening at the centers in their communities.

CoreCivic said last week the U.S. bought a 1,600-bed detention center in Minnesota that had been dormant for 16 years and a 1,033-bed Midwest Regional Reception Center in Leavenworth, Kansas, for a combined $734 million. The company also got a five-year contract to manage the Minnesota center that will bring in an estimated $75 million annually.

In early July, the company announced a $1.5 billion sale to the U.S. of the 2,560-bed California City Detention Facility and the 1,994-bed Otay Mesa Detention Center in San Diego.

Through those sales, CoreCivic grew its cash on hand 10 times over, from $109 million at the end of June to $1.1 billion following the transactions, its chief financial officer, David Garfinkle, said during an earnings call Thursday.

“This is more liquidity than the company has ever had, and provides us with significant flexibility to execute our capital allocation strategy and growth plan,” Garfinkle said.

Meanwhile, the Geo Group is in the process of selling to the federal government several detention centers that Immigration and Customs Enforcement already uses, depending on whether the company can also secure long-term management contracts, George Zoley, founder and chair, said during a call with investors.

“We are pursuing a potential sale of the buildings, but we want to retain the business,” Zoley said. “We consider ourselves primarily a support services operator, and will place particular importance on our ability to continue our support services at any facility sold to ICE.”

Zoley referenced during the Thursday call ICE’s procurement process for new contracts for 5,500 beds in areas of Colorado, Washington, Florida and Pennsylvania, where the Geo Group currently runs detention centers.

A draft procurement package for the contracts for those facilities states that “more stringent state or local laws or regulations shall not apply,” Wired first reported.

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region

“The last step of the process is pricing on that existing facility for the next contract term,” Zoley said. “There's a mutual interest by us and ICE that this process hopefully be completed by the end of this quarter.”

The purchase of the facilities is one prong of ICE’s most recent actions to expand detention capacity as part of the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement. ICE has also recently moved to start operations at idle prisons and contract companies to build more housing units across the country, outlined in documents posted in a federal contracting database in July.

Immigration rights advocates expect that the private detention center sales will thwart efforts at the state and local level to ensure safe conditions for detainees. The sales in San Diego and Leavenworth, Kansas, took place in areas where CoreCivic and local officials have been involved in lawsuits over oversight capabilities.

The Leavenworth City Commission had granted a permit to CoreCivic in March to reopen the detention center under an agreement that included a $1 million payment and plans for a local review board.

But city officials didn’t know about CoreCivic’s $238 million sale of the site to DHS until Wednesday morning, when it was publicly announced, City Manager Scott Peterson said in a statement.

Commissioner Holly Pittman said she worries the city will no longer have access to the detention center. Neither CoreCivic nor ICE have said whether the terms under the permit would remain in place.

“My priority right now is preserving those safeguards to the fullest extent legally possible,” Pittman said. “I don't know with DHS buying that, what our special use permit looks like now.”

The Department of Homeland Security pointed to California’s approach to rein in the detention centers in a statement following CoreCivic’s announcement in July of its $1.5 billion sale of the California City and San Diego detention centers.

“The state’s sanctuary politicians continue to push legislation to outlaw or make private prisons financially infeasible,” Lauren Bis, DHS assistant secretary for public affairs, said in a statement to The Center Square. “Now, with federal ownership of these detention centers, which are crucial to ICE’s detention network on the West Coast, ICE retains the detention capacity needed to arrest, detain and remove illegal aliens.”

In the Geo Group’s previous earnings call in May, Zoley said ICE ownership of the sites was a “logical solution” to overcome Democratic state-level leadership wanting more oversight.

Todd Schulte, president of FWD.us, an immigration advocacy group, said giving up ownership of the real estate would normally be risky for the companies, but that the relationship with the current administration made it a lucrative deal.

“If you're a private company, you get the benefit of a big cash infusion, and you get the benefit of a long-term contract with your buddies,” Schulte said. “If you're the government, you get to say, ‘We're going to restrict oversight and access.’”

entries.title: A Judge Demanded More Info From the U.S. in a Secret Deportation Case
entries.summary: Lawyers for an Afghan woman say the government has refused to disclose classified evidence it claims to have against her.
entries.content:
Nazira Haji Zada will have to continue waiting in custody for at least much of this month as the Trump administration tries to make her the first person deported though a newly activated secret court.

The Alien Terrorist Removal Court on Monday postponed a hearing that is meant to determine whether Haji Zada, an Afghan woman who was arrested by the FBI last month, may be released as the case moves forward.

U.S. District Judge Joan Ericksen of Minnesota, who is overseeing the case in the untested court, scrapped plans to hold a hearing on Tuesday after defense lawyers told her they could not fairly argue for Haji Zada’s release if the government keeps withholding the evidence it claims to have against her.

The case raises novel constitutional questions, because the Justice Department is making accusations while claiming that the proof is classified and cannot be made public. The Justice Department activated the terrorist deportation court for the first time in the court's 30-year existence.

Federal defenders Mary Petras and Matthew Farley wrote in a filing Friday that the government told them it would not turn over classified evidence without an order from the court. The government’s hard-line stance was forcing them to walk into Tuesday’s hearing “completely blind … without having had any opportunity to review or challenge the evidence that is being presented in favor of her continued detention.”

They called it a “blatant violation” of the Constitution’s Fifth Amendment for Haji Zada, who had been in the United States as a legal permanent resident, and a violation of the law that created the ATRC.

In response, Ericksen ordered the Justice Department to detail “all unclassified facts” the government is using to justify her ongoing detention with an eye toward public disclosure — but also to separately catalog each item it considers classified evidence and why disclosing it to defense attorneys would be a national security risk.

Ericksen gave the DOJ until Friday to comply with her order, and she gave defense lawyers another week to respond — all but ensuring that Haji Zada remains behind bars through most of August.

Haji Zada is currently listed as “Inmate 400151” at a D.C. jail. The D.C. Department of Corrections does not allow her to have any visitations, according to its online portal.

Court filings from her defense lawyers say she was arrested by FBI agents who showed up at her Fort Worth, Texas, home before dawn on July 28, and she was then forced onto a plane to the nation’s capital.

Her defense lawyers say she spent another two nights “without access to her family or legal counsel” in the D.C. jail’s notorious Central Cell Block — a temporary jail at Metropolitan Police Department headquarters which has been criticized for poor conditions and described by another local defense lawyer as a “living hellhole.”

A DOJ press release last week said Haji Zada was “being removed for her role in a plot to commit an ISIS-inspired mass shooting on Election Day in 2024.” Her son, Abdullah Haji Zada, is serving a 15-year sentence at a federal prison in Southern California after pleading guilty of receiving a firearm to commit terrorism.

Her son-in-law, Nasir Ahmad Tawhedi, has also pleaded guilty but was judicially ordered to receive mental treatment after a psychological evaluation. However, she was never criminally charged in those cases.

Instead, the DOJ elected to put Nazira Haji Zada through what is essentially a civil deportation proceeding — except one led by criminal prosecutors at the department’s National Security Division.

A prepared statement by Attorney General Todd Blanche said “allegations in this case show the matriarch of an ISIS-sympathizing family aiding in a plot to launch a mass casualty attack on American voters on Election Day.” An unclassified FBI summary claims that Nazira Haji Zada and Tawhedi “worked to indoctrinate her children with ISIS ideology and have them pledge loyalty to ISIS.”

The DOJ press release claimed that Nazira Haji Zada “signed a contract to sell the family house” — a reference to the previous allegation against her son and son-in-law that they had planned to use the funds to buy AK-47s to conduct some sort of attack.

However, in that criminal case, defense attorneys argued that the FBI accusation on the sale of the house is based on telegram conversations between Tawhedi and an alleged ISIS recruiter, and Tawhedi later admitted the statements were false during an FBI interview.

Property records show that the house was ultimately not sold and still belongs to the family.

entries.title: DOJ Sues to Stop In-State Tuition for Undocumented Students in Three States
entries.summary: The Department of Justice filed lawsuits against New York, Connecticut and Vermont in the latest effort to claw back protections and benefits for undocumented students.
entries.content:
The Department of Justice filed lawsuits against New York, Connecticut and Vermont on Monday for allowing undocumented students to receive in-state tuition — and vowed to keep pushing to end the practice nationwide.

Seventeen states have already faced legal challenges over state laws that give undocumented immigrants access to financial assistance programs.

The DOJ argues that the state programs in question unconstitutionally discriminate against students with U.S. citizenship — although New York, Connecticut and Vermont all offer in-state tuition reductions to all students who meet certain state residency requirements.

“Our efforts will not cease until President Trump’s promise is fulfilled: illegal aliens will not receive benefits denied to our Nation’s own citizens,” Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward said in a statement.

The Trump administration prevailed in some of its prior lawsuits, and multiple states have halted their tuition policies, including Texas, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Nebraska and Illinois.

Some of the lawsuits led to the end of programs started by decades-old state laws, like the Texas Dream Act, which passed with bipartisan support in 2001.

Woodward said the Justice Department has “now sued every state in the Second Circuit that seeks to thwart Congress’s clear prohibition by placing alien over citizen.”

The university systems for New York, Connecticut and Vermont did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the new legal challenges from the Trump administration.

Approximately 2.4% of all students enrolled in U.S. colleges and universities are undocumented, according to an October report from the Higher Ed Immigration Portal. Nearly 28% of those undocumented students are estimated to have or be eligible for Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, a program that provides temporary work permits and protection from deportation for individuals who came to the U.S. as children.

entries.title: An Army Under Secretary Purchased Stock in a Major Defense Contractor
entries.summary: A spokesperson says Michael Obadal’s purchase of SpaceX shares doesn’t conflict with his public duties.
entries.content:
SpaceX celebrated its initial public offering in June by selling hundreds of millions of shares — and making Elon Musk a trillionaire.

Among the buyers that day: Army Undersecretary Michael Obadal, who purchased between $1,001 and $15,000 worth of SpaceX stock, according to a financial disclosure document filed with the Office of Government Ethics and reviewed by NOTUS.

SpaceX does billions of dollars’ worth of business with the Department of Defense and the Space Force, including winning a $4.16 billion deal with the Space Force in May. The company does not hold contracts with the Army.

Maj. Pete Nguyen, an Army spokesperson, said Obadal purchased his SpaceX stock using Charles Schwab’s standard online brokerage platform as any member of the public could.

The exact value of Obadal’s SpaceX shares, which he did not specify, remains “well below the de minimis value exemption for the purposes of conflicts of interest” as outlined in federal law, Nguyen said. (Government officials are only required to report their stock-trade values in broad ranges.)

“Under Secretary Obadal is in full compliance with all federal financial disclosure and ethics rules,” Nguyen said. “Under Secretary Obadal has not had any professional or personal interactions with SpaceX, its employees, or officials. He continues to be committed to avoiding conflicts of interest as they pertain to his official duties.”

Obadal is responsible for “oversight of the Army’s business operations, manpower and personnel systems, acquisition strategy, and enterprise reform initiatives,” according to his official bio. In an ethics agreement Obadal signed prior to his 51-47 Senate confirmation in September, he vowed to take steps to “avoid any actual or apparent conflict of interest” and to resign from the government defense contractor Anduril Industries.

One government watchdog disagreed with the notion that buying and holding a defense contractor stock isn’t a conflict of interest for a top Army official.

“It’s ethically untenable for officials of federal agencies to be personally and financially invested in the fortunes of companies who do business with those agencies. Full stop,” said Dylan Hedtler-Gaudette, acting vice president of policy and government affairs for the nonprofit Project on Government Oversight.

“This is precisely why broad prohibitions on federal officials owning and trading stock while in their government positions are the only effective solution to both real and perceived corruption and conflicts of interest,” he continued.

Congress is actively considering whether to ban lawmakers and their immediate family members from buying individual stocks. A Republican-backed bill, the Stop Insider Trading Act, passed the House in July and now awaits consideration by the Senate.

Other stock-trading bills have sought to extend stock-trading prohibitions to top executive branch officials, but they have so far failed to gain enough support to trigger a vote.

Meanwhile, several top Trump administration officials have made notable personal financial trades or deals during recent months.

They include FBI Director Kash Patel, Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, Ambassador to Italy Tilman Fertitta, Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor, Federal Highway Administration Administrator Sean McMaster, U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro, Small Business Administration Administrator Kelly Loeffler, former U.S. Agency for Global Media leader Kari Lake, Department of Homeland Security Under Secretary Pedro Allende, Environmental Protection Agency Assistant Administrator Douglas Troutman and former Department of Health and Human Services general counsel Mike Stuart.

Trump himself has been the subject of significant scrutiny regarding the intersection of his personal finances and public service. The president has reported thousands of stock and bond trades during the past year and has routinely engaged in private crypto and other business ventures since returning to the White House in 2025.

entries.title: ‘Nothing Bad Can Happen’
entries.content:
Good afternoon. This is the Final NOTUS newsletter for Aug. 10, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

President Donald Trump signed an executive order reducing the number of recommended childhood vaccines and directing them to be administered during separate medical appointments “to the maximum extent feasible.”

  • “Nothing bad can happen from what we’re doing,” the president told reporters. He also said he broke his own children’s vaccinations up over several visits.
Trump is demanding compensation from Iran for damages, after Tehran over the weekend called for the U.S. to reimburse it for months of destruction. Trump said Iran “never mentioned” the request in any previous peace talks.

  • Iran should also be responsible for damages and deaths in Lebanon, Syria, Yemen and Gaza, Trump said. 
The U.S. emergency oil reserve has fallen below 300 million barrels, the lowest level recorded since the early 1980s, following the administration’s release of 172 million barrels in an attempt to stabilize oil prices that have risen with the conflict.





THE ADMINISTRATION

The Department of Homeland Security has spent more than $2.2 billion buying four immigration detention centers over the past two months.

Food manufacturers could have new Food and Drug Administration reporting requirements for additives under a new proposed rule.

The State Department said more than 175,000 visas have been revoked under Trump.





THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL

The deadline has passed for Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) to take his name off the ballot in the race for Ohio’s 7th Congressional District following accusations of domestic abuse, which he denies.

  • The National Electrical Contractors Association says it’s dumping Miller following NOTUS’ report about corporate and trade political committees that have donated to the congressman. “NECA will no longer support his campaign and has requested the return of our contribution” of $2,500, a NECA spokesperson confirmed.
The Democrat running for Senate in Montana, Alani Bankhead, refused to drop out of the race by this afternoon’s deadline to clear the way for independent candidate Seth Bodnar, who some Democrats think has a better chance of beating Republican Kurt Alme in the R+10 race.





THE STATES

Joint Base Charleston was officially renamed Joint Base Lindsey Graham. Pete Hegseth, Scott Bessent, Gov. Henry McMaster and Sen. Darline Graham attended the ceremony.

New York, Connecticut and Vermont are the latest states to face lawsuits from the DOJ for allowing undocumented students to receive in-state tuition.



BETH 2.0
